Right to Win

A right to win is not a property of a company. It is a relation between a company, one arena, one named rival and one moment in time — and the arithmetic of that relation is stranger, and less flattering, than most strategy memos admit.

1. Two Rooms, One Rival, Eighteen Days Apart

On the afternoon of 18 September 2026, in a low-ceilinged conference room at Charudatt Instruments' Hinjewadi campus in Pune, Ashwin Kelkar was asked a question he had been quietly dreading for eleven weeks. Charudatt had been building inline milk analysers since 1994. By FY26 it turned over ₹310 crore: ₹268 crore of instruments at a 31% gross margin, and ₹42 crore of software and annual maintenance contracts at 74%. Eleven thousand four hundred analysers sat in 2,900 village collection centres and 61 dairy processing plants; 214 field engineers covered nine states, calibrating those instruments on the ninety-day cycle that Legal Metrology verification requires. Ashwin, forty-four, an instrumentation engineer by training and senior vice-president of product by accident of survival, had proposed that Charudatt build Uptime — a plant-level predictive-maintenance and yield-loss analytics subscription — for ₹24.6 crore over twenty months. The chairman's question was the only one that mattered: "Against Chinmayan, what exactly do we have that they cannot buy?"

Chinmayan Systems was a four-year-old Hyderabad company that had raised the rupee equivalent of ₹1,160 crore to build a sensor-agnostic industrial anomaly-detection layer. It was live in fourteen plants across cement, steel and speciality chemicals at ₹41 lakh per plant per year, and in March 2026 it had opened three dairy pilots. It had more capital than Charudatt had revenue, better machine-learning talent than Charudatt could hire in Pune, and no legacy hardware business to protect. What Ashwin had was seven years of time-series readings — 2.4 crore data points a month — and 1,842 confirmed compressor and homogeniser failure events with maintenance-log ground truth attached. Whether that constituted a right to win, or merely an asset that felt like one, was the ₹24.6 crore question.

Eighteen days later, on 6 October 2026, Devika Menon faced a structurally identical question with almost none of the same facts. Menon was co-founder and chief product officer of Chitrangi Commerce, a Gurugram marketplace for wedding services — photographers, caterers, decorators, venues, makeup artists — with 71,000 verified vendors and 2.3 lakh weddings transacted in FY26. Gross merchandise value across the category its vendors served was ₹4,850 crore; ₹3,290 crore of it actually routed through Chitrangi's booking rails, yielding ₹135 crore at a 4.1% take rate, with a further ₹64 crore from vendor promotion and lead generation. Total revenue ₹199 crore, contribution margin 38%. The uncomfortable arithmetic sitting on Menon's desk was that the average Indian wedding on Chitrangi's platform spent about ₹9.6 lakh with vendors and routed only ₹1.43 lakh of it through Chitrangi. The platform touched fifteen per cent of the money and none of the deciding.

In June 2026 Chinmayan Systems — the same company, in a completely different disguise — had launched a consumer "life-event agent" that planned weddings, funerals, house moves and school admissions. By August, 19% of Chitrangi's new consumer sessions arrived carrying a budget sheet and a vendor shortlist generated somewhere else, up from 4% in March. Menon's proposal was Chitrangi Plan, an agentic planner of Chitrangi's own, at ₹31 crore over fourteen months. Her chief financial officer's objection was that between ₹23 crore and ₹29 crore of the ₹64 crore promotion line existed only because vendors bid for visibility, and an agent that confidently recommends three vendors destroys the auction that pays for it.

Two protagonists, two product types, one rival, and — this is the argument of the page — two completely different answers, arrived at by the same analysis. The purpose of what follows is not to teach the phrase "right to win." It is to show why a competent practitioner and an expert, looking at the same pair of memos, will disagree about which one is fundable, and to make the grounds of that disagreement explicit enough to referee.

2. The Idea: What It Is, Where It Came From, and Who Refuses to Sign It

Stated precisely: a right to win is a substantiated claim that, in a specifically bounded competitive arena, a firm possesses or can build capabilities and assets that make it more likely than named rivals to capture disproportionate economic value, and that those rivals cannot replicate quickly enough to erase the advantage before the firm has extracted the value. Four things in that sentence carry weight and are usually dropped: bounded arena, named rivals, economic value rather than revenue or share, and before — a clause about time, which is where the mathematics lives.

The phrase entered strategy practice through A.G. Lafley and Roger Martin's Playing to Win (2013), distilled from the Procter & Gamble strategy cascade, where it names the honest answer to the capability question inside a five-part chain of choices. But the intellectual problem it was invented to solve is older and sharper. Through the 1970s and 1980s, corporate planning had two failure modes running simultaneously: conglomerates entering arenas on the theory that good management was fungible, and business units justifying investment with market-attractiveness arguments that said nothing about the unit's own standing. Michael Porter's Competitive Strategy (1980) attacked the second by insisting that industry structure and a defensible, trade-off-bearing position determined returns. The resource-based view — Birger Wernerfelt in 1984, Jay Barney's VRIN criteria in 1991, C.K. Prahalad and Gary Hamel's "core competence" in 1990 — attacked the first by insisting that advantage originated inside the firm, in resources that were valuable, rare, imperfectly imitable and non-substitutable. George Stalk, Philip Evans and Lawrence Shulman's "Competing on Capabilities" (1992) bridged them by locating advantage in a small number of business processes executed distinctively well. Lafley and Martin's contribution was procedural rather than theoretical: they made the question answerable for one choice, by one team, on one page.

That lineage matters because the schools have not converged, and an expert must know which propositions each will and will not sign. The sharpest live disagreement is between the capability tradition and Hamilton Helmer's 7 Powers (2016), which holds that a capability qualifies as a source of advantage only if it constitutes both a benefit and a barrier — and that most things practitioners call capabilities are neither rare nor protected, and are competed away.

The practical consequence for Ashwin and Devika is that the same memo reads differently depending on the reader's school. A Porterian director asks Ashwin what Charudatt will stop doing to serve Uptime properly. A resource-based director asks how Charudatt acquired 1,842 labelled failure events below their replacement cost and whether the acquisition can be repeated by anyone else. A Helmer-trained director asks the hardest version: granted the labels are useful, what stops Chinmayan buying a year of maintenance records from three co-operative federations and closing 70% of the gap for ₹4 crore? That question turns out to have an answer, but not a comfortable one, and it is the subject of the next section.

3. Mechanics in Depth: The Half-Life of an Advantage

Competent practitioners establish that an advantage exists. Experts establish how fast it decays and how much can be collected before it does. The move that separates them is treating the advantage not as a binary state but as a stream with a time constant.

Formally, let G(t) be the annual economic advantage — the excess gross profit, in rupees per year, earned above what the same business would earn at competitive parity — at time t after entry. In arenas where imitation proceeds by accumulation rather than by a single discrete event, G decays approximately exponentially: G(t) = G0e−t/τ, where τ is the imitation time constant — the number of years in which a resourced rival closes the gap to 37% of its opening size. Discounting at the firm's cost of capital r, the present value of the advantage itself is the integral of the two exponentials, which collapses to a single clean expression:

PV of advantage = ∫0∞ G0e−t/τe−rt dt = G0 ÷ (1/τ + r)

The expression is worth staring at, because it says something counter-intuitive: the value of an advantage is not proportional to how big it is multiplied by how long you expect to hold it. It is the annual advantage divided by the sum of two decay rates — imitation and the cost of capital. When τ is short, the cost of capital barely matters and imitation dominates. When τ is long, the cost of capital becomes the binding constraint, which is why slow-moving, capital-intensive advantages in high-discount-rate markets are worth far less than the strategy deck implies.

Ashwin's team built G0 from the bottom up, per plant, and refused to count anything they could not tie to either a price the customer would pay or a cost the rival would incur. Two items survived. First, deployment cost: Chinmayan needed roughly ₹1.9 lakh of retrofit vibration and power-quality sensing plus ₹6.4 lakh of integration services per plant, because Indian dairy plants are thinly instrumented; Charudatt's analysers already sat on the measurement points and already back-hauled power and temperature telemetry, so its equivalent figures were ₹0.7 lakh and ₹1.8 lakh. The ₹5.8 lakh differential, amortised across a five-year contract, was worth ₹1.16 lakh a year. Second, a defensible price premium of 8% on the ₹14 lakh annual subscription — ₹1.12 lakh — justified by a lower false-alarm rate at ninety days. Total: ₹2.28 lakh per plant per year. At an expected year-three installed base of 96 plants under the wide-arena plan, G0 = ₹2.19 crore a year.

Estimating τ is the step teams skip, and it is the step that decides the answer. Charudatt's team estimated it three ways. Replacement cost: what would Chinmayan spend to assemble comparable labelled failure data? Roughly ₹6–9 crore and eighteen months of federation negotiations — real, but affordable for a company holding ₹1,160 crore. Accumulation rate: Chinmayan's three dairy pilots generated perhaps 40 labelled events a year each, against Charudatt's 1,842 already banked — but the gap in ratio terms narrows fast once the denominator grows. Observed narrowing: in cement, Chinmayan had gone from cold start to a validated alert in eleven weeks, because 92% of cement plants run a process historian with a decade of tag data; in dairy, only 74 of 441 plants had a historian at all. The three estimates converged on τ ≈ 3.5 years. Applying the formula at r = 16%, the present value of Charudatt's entire advantage came to ₹2.19 ÷ (0.286 + 0.16) = ₹4.9 crore.

Now the second-order effect that the formula makes unavoidable. Charudatt's entry cost was ₹24.6 crore. The advantage, fully valued, was worth ₹4.9 crore. A competent practitioner reads that and concludes the project is dead. The expert reads it correctly: a right to win is not the business case; it is the probability weight on the business case. The advantage does two economically distinct things, and conflating them is the single most common analytical error in this topic. It adds a margin stream worth ₹4.9 crore — and, far more importantly, it raises the probability that Charudatt captures the arena's base economics at all, which under the wide plan the team valued at a present value of about ₹48 crore of gross profit. Without the advantage, Charudatt assessed its chance of holding the arena against Chinmayan at 28%; with it, 58%. The thirty-point swing on ₹48 crore is ₹14.4 crore. Add the ₹4.9 crore. Expected value ₹19.3 crore against ₹24.6 crore of cost: negative ₹5.3 crore.

The step that follows is where the mechanics become a craft rather than a calculation. Ashwin did not abandon the arena; he re-cut it. The wide arena comprised all 441 Indian dairy plants intaking two lakh litres a day or more. But the ₹5.8 lakh deployment advantage only existed where Charudatt already owned the measurement points — its own 61 plants, plus 128 more where it held collection-centre telemetry upstream of the plant. Narrowing to those 189 plants let the team drop the ₹4.8 crore of retrofit-sensor engineering and certification required to serve strangers' hardware, cutting investment to ₹16.9 crore. In the narrower arena, penetration assumptions rose and the win probability rose further, because the arena had been defined around the place where the advantage was concentrated.

What made the narrow case fundable was a fourth term the original memo had omitted entirely, and which we return to in section 9: the defensive value. If Chinmayan established the analytics layer inside Charudatt's own 61 plants, the plant engineer's daily screen would become Chinmayan's, and the ₹42 crore software-and-AMC base would renew into a different vendor's ecosystem over the following four years. The team's estimate of the present value at risk was ₹11–19 crore. Right-to-win analysis run only offensively — as a question about arenas one might enter — systematically misses the arenas one cannot afford to lose.

4. Conditions, Stated as Testable Claims

The idea applies when five claims hold. Each is falsifiable, and each can be applied to both protagonists, which is the only honest way to show where the framework earns its keep and where it misleads.

Claim one: the arena can be bounded such that two competent analysts, given the description, would name the same competitor set. For Ashwin this held after the narrowing, though not comfortably; "plants where Charudatt owns the measurement points" is an arena described by Charudatt's own footprint, which is a warning sign we take up below. For Devika it failed at the first attempt. "Wedding planning" contains at least four arenas with different rivals — inspiration and discovery, budget and plan construction, vendor matching and booking, and execution-day coordination — and Chinmayan contested only the second. The entire strategic error available to Menon was to answer a question about arena two with an asset built for arena three.

Claim two: the buyer can perceive the difference at the moment of choice. This is the condition most often assumed rather than tested, and it admits a number. In the attraction model used by practitioners who have thought about this carefully, a firm's share is proportional to d · vβ, where v is its delivered value relative to the rival, d is the strength of its default position at the moment of choice, and β measures how sharply buyers discriminate on perceived value — effectively, how well they can tell the difference before committing. Charudatt estimated β ≈ 3.4 from 43 head-to-head deals in adjacent instrument categories. Chitrangi estimated β ≈ 1.1 from a 2025 experiment in which a shortlist that users rated 22% better produced only 5.4% more bookings. The same 18% value advantage converts to 64% share in Ashwin's arena and 54% in Devika's.

Claim three: the advantage's decay constant τ is long relative to the payback period. Charudatt's τ of 3.5 years against a payback of roughly 2.6 years in the narrow case clears, barely. Devika's would not: an agentic planner's quality advantage in a market where frontier model capability is improving quarterly has a τ her team could not credibly put above eighteen months.

Claim four: the advantage is asymmetric in the rival's costs, not merely absent from the rival's product. An advantage a rival could match by simply deciding to is a schedule, not a barrier. Charudatt's holds: for Chinmayan to serve a thinly instrumented dairy plant at Charudatt's cost, it would have to build a rural field-service network whose economics require density Chinmayan does not have. Chitrangi's liquidity — 71,000 vendors with availability, pricing and dispute history — is genuinely asymmetric, but only in the matching arena.

Claim five: winning the arena is worth winning. Right-to-win analysis is silent on arena attractiveness and will happily validate a decisive victory in a shrinking margin pool. This is where the framework is actively misleading rather than merely incomplete. It is at its most dangerous in three situations: when the contested margin pool is being competed away by a third party neither rival has named; when the advantage is real but the arena is a feature that a platform will absorb; and, most subtly, when the analysis is run on an arena defined so as to make the firm's asset decisive, producing a true claim about a market that does not exist independently of the claimant.

5. Hard Edge Cases: Multi-Product, Two-Sided, Regulated, Hardware-Plus-Software, AI-Native

The clean version of the analysis assumes one firm, one arena, one buyer. Every one of those assumptions breaks in practice, and the breakages are where experienced practitioners spend their time.

Multi-product firms face an allocation problem the framework does not contain. A capability is not a stock that can be drawn down simultaneously by three business units. Charudatt's data-science group numbered nine people; committing seven to Uptime meant the analyser firmware roadmap lost its only two machine-learning engineers. Mature companies handle this with an internal register — several large Indian industrial groups keep something like an "advantage ledger," a list of the firm's genuine asymmetries with an owner, a review date and, crucially, a list of the units that have a claim on each. What such firms actually do, as opposed to what their strategy documents say, is ration the ledger by seniority and adjacency, and the second-order effect is that a new arena adjacent to a powerful unit gets the capability and an equally promising arena adjacent to a weak unit does not.

Two-sided businesses have two rights to win and usually only examine one. Chitrangi's memo analysed the consumer side. Its actual asymmetry sat on the vendor side: 71,000 vendors with four years of completion, cancellation and dispute history. That asset is worthless against an agent that never needs vendor supply because it stops at advice, and decisive against one that must eventually book something. The expert question in a two-sided market is not "do we have an advantage" but "on which side does the contested transaction terminate, and do we own that side?"

Regulated arenas can convert a cost into a barrier, but only where the regulator's requirement is specific to incumbency. Charudatt's Legal Metrology verification licences and its ninety-day calibration obligation are, on the face of it, a compliance burden. In practice they mandate a field visit every quarter that a rival must either duplicate at ₹6,200 a visit or do without. Here regulation is a genuine source of asymmetry. For Chitrangi, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's consent requirements cut the other way: using four years of booking history to train a planner required consent that a new entrant, collecting fresh consent at signup, obtains more cleanly than an incumbent re-papering old records. Regulation is not a moat; it is a cost imposed on everyone, which becomes a moat only where the incumbent's cost of compliance is structurally lower.

Hardware-plus-software raises the problem of which layer holds the advantage — and the answer migrates. Charudatt's advantage in 2019 lived in hardware placement and field service. By 2026 the plant engineer's daily attention had moved to a screen, and whoever owned the screen would eventually specify the hardware. The seam is organisational as much as technical: Charudatt's instrument division was measured on unit margin and its software group on ARR, and the transfer price between them had never been agreed, which meant that the very question of whether to subsidise a sensor kit to win a subscription had no forum in which it could be decided. This is typical. Advantage dies at seams far more often than it dies in the market.

AI-native situations invert the usual timing. Traditionally, capability was slow to build and slow to copy. Foundation models make a certain class of capability fast to build and fast to copy simultaneously, which compresses τ without compressing the build cost. The durable asymmetry, where one exists, is almost never the model and almost never the raw data; it is a closed loop — a workflow that produces a labelled outcome quickly and cheaply enough that the system improves at a rate the rival cannot match. Charudatt's loop existed: a maintenance engineer closing a work order labels the prediction within days. Chitrangi's did not: a wedding's ground truth arrives once, months later, from a customer who never returns.

The hardest seam of all surfaced in Charudatt's legal review. The 1,842 labelled failure events lived in customer plants, and only 38 of 61 plant contracts granted Charudatt analytics rights over the data. The asset the entire memo rested on was, in a third of cases, someone else's. Renegotiating those 23 contracts was possible but would signal precisely what Charudatt intended — which brings us to a nuance in the next section that most practitioners learn the expensive way.

6. Ten Things That Separate an Expert from a Competent Practitioner

First, experts test asymmetry in the rival's cost structure, not absence from the rival's product. The competent question is "can they do this?"; the expert question is "what would it cost them, and what would it cost them to keep doing it?" The tell-tale sign in the wild is a memo whose competitive section is a feature comparison table. The obvious reading — we have three features they lack — is wrong because features are schedules, not barriers; the correct reading asks what a rival would have to give up. Chinmayan could match Charudatt's deployment cost only by building a rural service network whose fixed cost is recoverable only at a density Chinmayan cannot reach, which is why the advantage is real.

Second, the contested unit is the margin pool, not revenue or share. Teams celebrate share gains in arenas where price has collapsed. The tell is a plan in which revenue grows and gross margin per unit falls, described as "scaling." The obvious reading, that share is the leading indicator of eventual profit, is wrong in any arena where the marginal competitor prices at its own marginal cost — increasingly common where a capable substitute has near-zero marginal cost. Devika's team found that the ₹64 crore promotion line was the only part of Chitrangi's revenue with a defensible margin, and it was the part the new product would damage.

Third, experts distinguish a stock of advantage from a rate of advantage. A stock — data collected, plants installed, brand recognition earned — depreciates and is copyable at a price. A rate — a loop that improves faster than the rival's — compounds. The tell is what happens under competitive pressure: a stock advantage narrows when a rival invests; a rate advantage widens. The obvious reading treats a large stock as safety, when in fact a large stock with no loop attached is exactly the asset a well-funded rival buys.

Fourth, watch for advantage that lives on someone else's balance sheet. Exclusive channel arrangements, preferential supplier terms, a favourable model-provider contract, or in Charudatt's case data rights held under 38 of 61 customer agreements. The tell is that the enabling contract has a renewal date inside the investment's payback period. The obvious reading — we have it locked up — is wrong because what is locked up is a term, not a right, and the counterparty's incentive at renewal is precisely to sell the same term to your rival.

Fifth, the rival you name is rarely the rival who takes the arena. Naming a competitor is a discipline, but it has its own failure mode: it anchors the analysis on the most visible threat rather than on the lowest-cost entrant. The expert runs a different test — who has the lowest incremental cost of entering this arena, given assets they already hold for another purpose? For Chitrangi, the answer was not Chinmayan; it was any platform already holding the consumer's attention at the moment the wedding is announced. The tell is a competitive section that lists three companies in the same category and none from adjacent ones.

Sixth, an advantage must survive the organisational seam at which it will be consumed. A capability owned by a shared platform team is not available to a business unit; it is available subject to arbitration. The tell-tale sign is a plan whose critical path runs through a team whose quarterly commitments do not mention it. The obvious reading — the capability exists inside the company — is wrong because the relevant question is whether it exists inside the plan, in writing, with a named owner and a date.

Seventh, value created and value captured are governed by different variables, and β is the bridge. A product that saves a plant ₹80 lakh a year may capture ₹14 lakh or ₹2 lakh depending entirely on whether the buyer can verify the saving before purchase and whether an alternative claims the same. The tell is a business case built on customer ROI with no stated mechanism for why price does not fall to the next-best provider's cost. The obvious reading — we create enormous value, so we will capture a fair share — is wrong because capture is set by the buyer's alternatives, not by the size of the benefit.

Eighth, "we have the data" is almost never the advantage; the label loop is. The expert's diagnostic is three questions asked in sequence: where does ground truth come from, how long does it take to arrive, and who pays for it? Charudatt's answers were the maintenance work order, four to nine days, and the customer's own technician — a near-ideal loop. Chitrangi's were a post-event survey, eleven months, and Chitrangi itself, at a response rate of 12%. The tell is a data section that quotes volume. Volume is the least informative property of a dataset.

Ninth, experts write the rival's memo before writing their own. The exercise is not rhetorical. Ashwin's team produced a two-page document titled "Why Chinmayan wins dairy," and the strongest sentence in it — that Chinmayan need not beat Charudatt at all, only reach good-enough accuracy at a price that makes the category a commodity before Charudatt's payback completes — reframed the entire timing discussion. The tell of a team that has not done this is a memo in which the rival has no strategy, only a product.

Tenth, an advantage that requires a sustained choice the organisation has never sustained is an aspiration. Richard Rumelt's point about coherent action applies with force here: many right-to-win claims are true conditional on the firm holding a trade-off for eight consecutive quarters. The tell is a plan that requires saying no to something the company has historically said yes to — declining a large hardware order that conflicts with the subscription model, or refusing a vendor's promotion spend that the agent's recommendations would contradict. The obvious reading treats capability as the constraint; the real constraint is organisational persistence, and it is empirically much scarcer.

7. How the Picture Changes by Product Type and by Stage

Some of the differences across product types are real and some are folklore, and it is worth separating them.

In consumer products, β is typically low: buyers cannot evaluate quality before consumption, decide quickly, and are heavily influenced by default placement. The practical consequence is that a consumer right to win built on product superiority is fragile unless it converts into habit or brand memory fast; the durable consumer asymmetries are distribution, default placement and the cost of acquiring the next customer. Devika's arena is this case, and the honest reading of Exhibit 3b is that Chitrangi cannot win an advice arena on advice quality.

In B2B and enterprise, β is higher because a procurement process exists specifically to raise it, but the decision unit fragments: the person who perceives the value, the person who bears the switching cost and the person who signs are often three people with different objective functions. A right to win in enterprise must therefore be stated per stakeholder. Charudatt's advantage was strongest with the plant engineer and weakest with the group CFO, for whom a subscription line was a new cost where hardware had been capital expenditure — a difference that cost Ashwin two of his first six trials.

In platforms and marketplaces, the difference is genuine and structural: advantage is a function of liquidity, and liquidity is local. Chitrangi had liquidity in Delhi NCR, Jaipur and Hyderabad wedding supply and almost none in Kerala. A national right-to-win claim in a marketplace is nearly always an average concealing a set of city-level truths, some of which are decisive and most of which are not.

In hardware and physical goods, the τ is long — supply chains, tooling, certification and field networks all take years to copy — but so is the firm's own response time, which means hardware advantages are durable and hardware disadvantages are equally durable. This symmetry is underappreciated. Charudatt's field network gave it eight years of protection in telematics and simultaneously guaranteed that its cost base could not be reduced quickly when a lighter competitor arrived.

In AI products, the difference commonly asserted — that everything is commoditised — is mostly false, and the difference that is real is rarely stated. Model quality converges; what does not converge is access to a workflow where outcomes are observed. The honest statement is that AI compresses τ for capabilities expressed as model quality, leaves τ roughly unchanged for capabilities expressed as distribution and regulatory position, and in some cases lengthens it for capabilities expressed as proprietary label loops, because the loop's advantage compounds.

Stage changes the analysis less than product type but changes its honest use more. An early-stage company rarely has assets; its claim rests on insight and speed, and its correct posture is to treat the right-to-win memo as a hypothesis with a named expiry rather than as a justification. A scaled company has assets and an attention constraint; its failure mode is assuming that an advantage built for one arena transfers. A very large company has both, plus a third problem: its advantages are visible, documented and therefore targetable. Charudatt's 2019 telematics win happened partly because nobody outside the dairy belt noticed it for three years. Its 2026 entry would be announced at a trade fair, which shortens τ for free.

8. Three Worked Examples

The one that worked: cold-chain telematics, 2019–2022

Charudatt's own best example predates the current debate. In 2019 it entered chilling-centre telematics — remote temperature and power monitoring for village-level milk chilling units — against two software entrants with better user interfaces and lower prices. The arena was 3,150 chilling centres across three co-operative federations. Charudatt's subscription was ₹38,000 per centre per year, roughly 20% above the entrants'. It won 2,140 centres, 68% of the arena, for ₹8.1 crore of ARR at a 61% contribution margin.

The right to win was not the product. It was that Legal Metrology verification required a physical calibration visit every ninety days, Charudatt's engineers were already making it, and the marginal cost of adding a telematics service call to an existing route was ₹1,450 against a standalone entrant's ₹6,200. At a ₹38,000 price point, a ₹4,750 per-visit cost difference across four annual visits was ₹19,000 — half the revenue. The entrants could not price below Charudatt and survive, and could not build a comparable route density without the calibration mandate that justified it. τ was approximately eight years. The lesson Ashwin carried into 2026 was the correct one: the advantage was in the rival's cost structure, not in Charudatt's feature list.

The one that failed: Chitrangi Photos, 2022–2024

In November 2022 Chitrangi launched a cloud gallery and client-proofing product for its photographer vendors, reasoning that with 71,000 vendors already on the platform it had a distribution right to win. The plan assumed 15% attach at ₹9,600 a year — ₹10.2 crore of ARR. It reached 1,740 vendors, 2.4%, with 61% first-year churn and ₹1.4 crore of revenue, and was shut in September 2024 after ₹19 crore had been spent.

The post-mortem found two errors, one obvious and one not. The obvious error was that the arena's key success factors were storage cost per rupee and proofing speed, on neither of which Chitrangi had any asymmetry; free and near-free alternatives existed. The non-obvious error was that Chitrangi's relationship was with the studio owner in his capacity as a seller of services, while the purchase decision for a delivery tool sat with the post-production lead — the same counterparty, a different buyer. The capability had been matched to the wrong person inside the right company, which is a failure mode no feature comparison detects.

The recovery is the instructive part. Rather than concluding that Chitrangi had no adjacent right to win, the team re-ran the match test on every asset and found one that had never been on the original list: four years of completion, cancellation and dispute data across 2.3 lakh weddings constituted an underwriting signal no lender possessed. Chitrangi Settle — instant payout advances to vendors against confirmed bookings, in partnership with an RBI-regulated lending partner — advanced ₹640 crore in FY26 at a 1.9% net take, ₹12.2 crore of revenue, with a realised loss rate of 0.42% against an unsecured small-business benchmark several times that. Fourteen of the twenty-one Photos engineers moved onto it. The asset had been there all along; what had been wrong was the description of it. Chitrangi had called it "vendor relationships" when it was in fact "verified completion history."

The third example is the one Ashwin's team built about their opponent, and it demonstrates that the same firm's right to win varies more across arenas than across competitors.

Two of these deserve elaboration because they are the ones that damaged real decisions in this case. The seventh — running the analysis only offensively — is the most expensive and the least discussed. Every framing in the literature poses the question as "where should we play?", which produces memos about arenas one might enter. The dual question, "which arena would it be catastrophic for us to lose?", uses the identical machinery and yields a different answer, because the relevant comparison is not the arena's standalone value but the present value of the base business under two futures. Charudatt's ₹16.9 crore narrow-arena case cleared by ₹1.7 crore as an offensive investment and by something between ₹13 crore and ₹21 crore once the ₹11–19 crore of at-risk AMC value was counted. The board approved it on the defensive number, which is the honest reason, and Ashwin insisted the memo say so — because a project justified on the wrong number will be measured on the wrong number, and Uptime's first-year success metric ought to be renewal retention in the 61 plants rather than new-logo wins.

The sixth — announcing the advantage — is the one practitioners find hardest to believe until it happens. The go-to-market narrative that best sells the product ("seven years of dairy-specific failure data no one else has") is precisely the instruction manual for closing the gap. There is a genuine ethical line here and it is worth naming: describing the benefit precisely while describing the mechanism generally is fair; claiming a mechanism you do not have is not.

10. Where Experts Genuinely Disagree

Four disagreements in this topic are live, and none of them is resolved by a synthesis that anyone actually holds.

Is a capability ever a right to win? Helmer's position, in its strongest form, is that the vast majority of what firms call capabilities are competitively arbitraged: if a capability is valuable and a rival can hire, buy or build it at a cost proportionate to its value, no excess return survives. On this view Charudatt's data advantage is not a power at all; it is a two- or three-year head start with a price tag on it, and calling it a right to win encourages exactly the overinvestment the ₹24.6 crore wide case represented. The capability school's reply, in its strongest form, is that imitation costs are empirically far higher than the arbitrage argument assumes — tacit knowledge, organisational routines and customer-embedded workflow all impose costs that do not appear on any acquisition price — and that Helmer's criterion, applied strictly, would have declared Charudatt's telematics position unworthy of investment in 2019, when it in fact produced eight years of protected margin. What would have to be true for Helmer to be wrong in general: imitation lags in real industries would have to be long enough that an advantage with no formal barrier still yields returns well above cost of capital, which the telematics case supports and the dairy-analytics case, at τ = 3.5 years and r = 16%, does not.

Is the arena discovered or designed? The rival-relative test requires a named competitor and a bounded arena, and category-design advocates argue this is exactly how firms trap themselves inside a frame the incumbent defined. Their strongest evidence is that the largest value creations of the past three decades occurred in categories that did not exist when the company started, where any honest right-to-win memo would have had no competitor to name. The rival-relative camp's strongest reply is survivorship: for every category creator, a large number of firms declared a new category, faced no named rival, and discovered that the reason no rival existed was that no margin pool did. Devika's decision sits precisely on this fault line, and it is genuinely unclear which camp is right about her case.

Does proprietary data still confer advantage? One camp holds that model capability convergence has made data moats largely illusory: the marginal value of a proprietary corpus falls as general models improve, and most firms' data is smaller, dirtier and more redundant than they believe. The other holds that the relevant asset was never the corpus but the loop, and that loops embedded in workflows with fast, cheap ground truth are becoming more valuable as models commoditise, because the model is no longer the differentiator and the feedback is. Both camps can point at Charudatt's 1,842 labelled events and reach opposite conclusions: the first notes that Chinmayan can buy equivalent records for ₹6–9 crore, the second that buying the records does not buy the work-order integration that produces the next 1,842.

Should early-stage firms run the analysis at all? The entrepreneurial objection is that at seed stage the analysis is theatre, since advantage is discovered through operating and most successful positions were not foreseeable ex ante. The counter is that the analysis is not a forecast but a discipline for spending less money on claims that were already falsifiable — and that the cost of running it is a week. The disagreement is real and turns on an empirical question nobody has settled: how much of the variance in early-stage outcomes is attributable to positions that were identifiable in advance.

The unresolved questions are not decoration. A practitioner who cannot state which side of each of these four they are on, and why, will produce memos whose conclusions depend on whoever wrote them rather than on the evidence.

11. What Mastery Looks Like

Someone who has merely studied this topic writes a good competitive section. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways.

They quantify decay before they quantify size. Asked about an advantage, they ask how long it lasts before they ask how big it is, because the second number without the first is uninterpretable. They will put a number on τ and defend it from at least two independent estimates — replacement cost and observed narrowing — rather than asserting durability.

They separate the probability weight from the value. They will not let a memo claim that the right to win justifies the investment; they insist on the decomposition, because the decomposition is what reveals when an advantage is real and still insufficient, which is the most common true state of the world and the one that most often gets papered over.

They write the opponent's memo, and they narrow arenas rather than abandoning them. When the numbers fail, their instinct is not "no" but "where inside this is the advantage concentrated enough to clear?" — while remaining honest that narrowing can degenerate into gerrymandering, and applying the customer-recognition test to their own narrowing.

And they instrument the claim. A mastered right-to-win memo names the two or three observable quantities that would falsify it — for Charudatt, false-alarm rate at week twenty and whether Chinmayan acquires an instrumentation company; for Chitrangi, the share of new sessions arriving with an externally generated plan — and puts them on a dashboard with a review date. The memo becomes a monitored hypothesis rather than an artefact of a planning cycle. That, more than any framework literacy, is what a board is actually buying.

12. What They Decided

Ashwin Kelkar recommended the narrow arena, at ₹16.9 crore, justified explicitly on defensive grounds: the objective was to keep the plant engineer's screen, and by extension the ₹42 crore software-and-AMC base, rather than to capture 441 plants. He committed to two pre-conditions before the second tranche: renegotiating analytics rights in at least 18 of the 23 deficient plant contracts, and reaching a false-alarm rate below 0.5 per week at six trial plants within twenty weeks. He also told the board, in writing, that if Chinmayan acquired an instrumentation business the τ assumption collapsed and the programme should be reviewed within thirty days rather than at the next annual cycle.

Devika Menon did not fund Chitrangi Plan as proposed. Her reading of Exhibit 3b was that a better planner, in an arena with β near 1.1 and a rival holding a substantially stronger default at the moment a wedding is announced, buys share she could not hold and costs her the promotion revenue that funds the company. She proposed instead to spend ₹9 crore making Chitrangi's vendor supply — availability, real prices, dispute history — accessible to any planning agent, including Chinmayan's, on commercial terms, on the argument that Chitrangi's genuine asymmetry terminated at the booking and that an advice layer it did not own was less dangerous than an advice layer that routed around it. Two of her five directors regarded this as capitulation dressed as strategy. The disagreement had not been settled when the meeting closed.

Question one. Ashwin narrowed his arena to the 189 plants where Charudatt already owned the measurement points. Is that a legitimate concentration of the analysis on where the advantage lives, or is it the gerrymandering failure mode in Exhibit 5 — an arena defined by the claimant's own footprint? What evidence would settle it, and who should be asked?

Question two. Devika's proposal makes Chitrangi's supply available to the rival contesting the layer above it. Under what conditions is supplying your competitor the correct expression of a right to win, and under what conditions is it the first step in becoming a commodity input? Which condition does Chitrangi satisfy?

Question three. Charudatt's programme was approved on a defensive number — ₹11 to ₹19 crore of at-risk existing revenue — while its plan, team and metrics were designed for offence. What specifically should change about how Uptime is staffed, priced and measured if the honest justification is defensive? And what does it say about the field that almost no right-to-win framework asks the defensive question at all?

13. Going Deeper

The product strategy document is where a right to win must physically live; a strategy document without a falsifiable advantage claim is a plan, and the discipline of writing the claim into the document is what forces the arena and the rival to be named. Moats and the 7 Powers supplies the strongest critique of everything above — the argument that a capability is not a power unless it is simultaneously a benefit and a barrier — and is the natural next reading for anyone who found section 10's first disagreement unresolved. Competing with open source and free matters because it models the extreme case of the β and price-floor problem: what happens to value capture when the next-best alternative has zero marginal cost and improves without you. Competitive analysis provides the evidence base the whole method depends on — win/loss data, deal histories, the head-to-head records from which β is estimated — and is the difference between a scored comparison and a guessed one. Network effects and switching costs and lock-in are the two mechanisms that most reliably lengthen τ, and knowing their failure conditions tells you when a long-τ assumption is unsafe. Moats in the AI era takes up the label-loop argument in detail and is where the third disagreement in section 10 is fought out with current evidence. Positioning is the discipline of making the advantage legible to a buyer, without which a real advantage converts at a low β. And five forces and industry structure answers the question right-to-win analysis deliberately brackets — whether the arena is worth winning at all — which, as Charudatt's ₹24.6 crore wide case shows, is the question that decides whether a genuine advantage is an opportunity or an expensive way to be right.

Right to Win

Why you can build something markedly better than what exists — and how to know, before you spend the money, whether that belief is a fact or a wish.

An ICU Module, a Board Meeting, and a Question Vaibhav Health Systems Had Never Had to Answer This Precisely

On the morning of 11 March 2026, Meera Chandrasekhar, vice-president of product at Vaibhav Health Systems, sat in her Indiranagar office in Bengaluru rewriting the same paragraph for the fourth time. It was the opening page of a board pre-read due by Thursday, and it was meant to answer a question the board had never made her answer this precisely before: not "is this a good product," not "is this a big market," but "why will Vaibhav win it, and win it against a named rival who is already inside the building."

The product in question was NeuroWatch, a module that would sit on top of Vaibhav's existing bed-management platform and flag ICU patients at risk of deterioration twelve to eighteen hours before a nurse would otherwise notice, using the vitals and nursing-note data Vaibhav's software already captured. Vaibhav's core platform — ward censuses, bed turnover, discharge planning — was live in 210 hospitals across Karnataka, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu, generating ₹42 crore of annual recurring revenue and renewing, on average, at 91%. NeuroWatch would be new: a predictive-analytics product competing directly with Vidisha Clinical Systems, a Chennai-founded company that had spent six years and, by industry estimate, upward of ₹60 crore building exactly this kind of deterioration-prediction tool, and that already held live contracts in 340 hospitals, more than half of them hospitals Vaibhav did not yet serve.

The stakes were not abstract. Building NeuroWatch properly — the machine-learning model, the clinical validation study a credible hospital would demand, the integration work, the sales enablement — would consume roughly ₹2.5 crore and nine months of a team Vaibhav could otherwise point at expanding the core platform into Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, markets with no Vaibhav presence and no Vidisha presence either. If Meera's team built NeuroWatch and lost to Vidisha anyway, Vaibhav would have spent close to 6% of its annual revenue proving a negative, in a market where two well-capitalised global players, Philips and GE Healthcare, were also extending their monitoring hardware into predictive software, and where a Bengaluru-based contactless-vitals company, Dozee, was already selling hospitals a version of the same promise. The question in front of Meera was not whether NeuroWatch was a good idea; good ideas were not scarce inside Vaibhav. What she owed the board was a specific, falsifiable answer to a narrower question: did Vaibhav have a right to win this particular arena, against these particular rivals, or was it about to spend nine months and real money finding out the hard way that it did not.

The Idea: A Claim You Have to Earn, Not Assert

A right to win is a substantiated, specific reason — grounded in capabilities and assets a company actually possesses — for believing it can capture disproportionate value in a chosen competitive arena, relative to the particular rivals contesting that arena, over a time horizon long enough for the advantage to matter. It is not a synonym for ambition and it is not a claim about the company in general; it is a claim about one arena, tested against one set of named competitors, at one point in time. A company can have a strong right to win in one arena and none at all in the arena next door.

The term, and the disciplined way of testing it, comes out of a specific strategy tradition rather than being loose business-school folklore. A.G. Lafley, chief executive of Procter & Gamble through most of the 2000s, and strategist Roger Martin, then dean of the Rotman School of Management, formalised it in their 2013 book Playing to Win, distilled from P&G's internal strategy process. Their framework poses five cascading questions a strategy must answer in order: what is our winning aspiration, where will we play, how will we win there, what capabilities must be in place, and what management systems will sustain them. "Right to win" is their name for the honest answer to the fourth question, tested against the third: not "how would we like to win" but "do we actually have, or can we credibly build, the specific capability that makes winning here more likely than not." The idea has an earlier ancestor, too — George Stalk, Philip Evans and Lawrence Shulman's 1992 Harvard Business Review article "Competing on Capabilities," which argued that sustainable advantage comes less from static market position than from a small number of business processes a company executes distinctively well across its whole portfolio. Lafley and Martin's contribution was to make that idea usable at the level of a single strategic choice: not "what are we good at in general" but "for this specific arena, against these specific rivals, what is our evidence."

The sentence Meera could say in the boardroom without sounding glib, and without overclaiming, was this: "We only have the right to enter an arena if we can name the one or two capabilities that make us more likely to win it than the specific rivals already there, and explain why those rivals cannot quickly copy them." That sentence does three pieces of work at once. It forces specificity about the arena. It forces the comparison to be against named competitors rather than the market in the abstract. And it forces a claim about durability — not just an advantage today, but one a rival cannot erase within the time it takes to matter.

How the Test Actually Runs

Practitioners who use "right to win" well are not reciting the phrase; they are running a specific sequence of tests, most of which are easy to state and easy to skip under deadline pressure. The sequence begins narrower than most teams expect, and it is worth walking through gate by gate, because the two gates people skip most often are exactly the two that separate a real right to win from a hopeful one.

Step one is defining the arena with enough precision that two people would identify the same set of competitors from the description. "Hospital software" is not an arena; "ICU deterioration-prediction software sold to tertiary-care private hospitals in India with more than 200 beds" is. Meera's team spent most of a week narrowing NeuroWatch's arena this way, because the honest answer to "who competes with us" changes completely depending on whether the arena includes government hospitals, includes hardware-bundled monitoring systems, or is confined to software sold as an add-on to an existing hospital-operations platform.

Step two is naming the arena's key success factors — the two or three things that actually determine who wins a deal or keeps a renewal, established from evidence rather than assumption. For NeuroWatch, Meera's team found, through conversations with eleven hospital chief medical officers, that the deciding factors were clinical trust (would a doctor act on the alert), integration friction (how much new hardware or workflow change the hospital had to absorb), and total cost of ownership including training time — not, as the product team had initially assumed, model accuracy in isolation, since every vendor claimed comparable accuracy and hospitals had no easy way to verify the claim before buying.

Step three is inventorying candidate capabilities and assets the company can bring to that specific arena — not a list of things the company is proud of, but a list of things that might plausibly move one of the named key success factors. For Vaibhav, the candidates were: an existing, already-trusted integration with the ward workflow in 210 hospitals; six years of clean vitals and nursing-note data from those hospitals that a cold-start entrant would not have; and an existing procurement relationship with the same hospital administrators who would need to sign off on any new module.

Step four, the one practitioners most often skip, is the match test: does each candidate capability actually move one of the named key success factors, or does it merely sound impressive? Vaibhav's existing integration mattered because it reduced integration friction, a named key success factor. Its six years of historical data mattered because it could shorten the validation study a clinical buyer would demand, addressing clinical trust faster than a cold-start rival could. Vaibhav's warm relationship with hospital administrators, by contrast, turned out not to matter much, because the CMOs Meera's team interviewed said the deterioration-alert purchase decision ran through the clinical committee, not the administrative one — a capability that felt relevant and, for this specific arena, was not.

Step five, skipped almost as often, is the relative-advantage test, run against the specific named rival rather than against a generic absence of competition: not "can we do this" but "can we do this better than Vidisha Clinical Systems can, given what Vidisha already has built." Step six is the durability test — estimating how long it would take a resourced rival to close the gap, since almost every advantage is copyable given enough time and capital; the real question is whether the company can extract enough value before that happens. Step seven, the economics test, asks whether pursuing the arena, even with a genuine advantage, generates more value than it costs to pursue — a right to win with a negative return is still a bad decision. Only after all seven does a team reach step eight: commit in full, stage the commitment to reduce risk, or decline the arena.

A Worked Example: Running the Arithmetic on NeuroWatch

Meera's team ran the economics test with real numbers, because the board would ask for them regardless of how the qualitative argument landed. NeuroWatch's engineering cost was straightforward to build up from the team plan: four senior engineers at a fully loaded annual cost of ₹32 lakh each, two clinical data scientists at ₹38 lakh each, and a part-time clinical-safety advisor retained at ₹24 lakh a year. Summed, that team cost ₹2.28 crore a year to run, or ₹19 lakh a month. At a nine-month build-and-validate timeline, the direct build cost came to ₹1.71 crore; adding a ₹60 lakh clinical validation study that three CMOs had told Meera's team they would require before trusting any deterioration alert, the total investment to reach a sellable NeuroWatch was ₹2.31 crore — close enough to the ₹2.5 crore Meera had quoted the board to be the same number in practice.

Against that cost, Meera's team modelled revenue two ways, because the entire logic of "right to win" lived in the gap between them. In the favourable case — the case that depended on NeuroWatch behaving, in the hospital's eyes, as an add-on to a system it already trusted rather than as a new purchase — the team assumed hospitals already on Vaibhav's core platform could adopt NeuroWatch through the existing procurement relationship, without a fresh vendor-evaluation cycle, at a price of ₹9 lakh per hospital per year. If 25% of Vaibhav's 210 existing hospitals attached NeuroWatch within the first twelve months — a conservative assumption, since attach rates on existing accounts commonly run higher — that produced 52.5 hospitals and ₹4.72 crore of incremental annual recurring revenue against a ₹2.31 crore investment: a payback inside six months, and an outcome Vidisha, selling cold into each hospital with no existing footprint, could not match on cost even if its model were equally accurate, because Vidisha's own customer-acquisition cost per hospital — a sales cycle of roughly nine months carrying a fully loaded rep cost of about ₹18 lakh per won hospital, by the estimate of two former Vidisha sales hires now at Vaibhav — sat well above Vaibhav's near-zero incremental distribution cost for the same hospital.

That was the arithmetic that made NeuroWatch look, on first pass, like a clear right to win: a genuine, matched, rival-relative cost advantage, not just an appealing product idea. But Meera made herself run a second pass before writing the board memo, because the favourable case rested entirely on one unverified assumption — that hospitals would in fact treat NeuroWatch as a low-friction add-on rather than routing it through the same clinical-committee evaluation a cold-start vendor would face. If that assumption was wrong — if, as one CMO had warned, "anything that touches an ICU alert goes through the full committee, existing vendor or not" — the picture changed sharply. A full committee cycle would push the validation and rollout timeline from nine months to roughly sixteen, since each hospital's own ethics and safety committee would want its own evidence review, lifting engineering cost to ₹3.04 crore before the ₹60 lakh study, for a total of ₹3.64 crore; it would also very likely cut the effective attach rate from 25% to something closer to 15%, since a fraction of hospitals evaluating a new clinical tool from scratch would also entertain Vidisha or Dozee rather than defaulting to Vaibhav. Fifteen percent of 210 hospitals, at the same ₹9 lakh price, produced ₹2.84 crore of incremental ARR in year one against ₹3.64 crore of investment — a payback of well over a year, and a case that no longer separated cleanly from a rival's economics.

The Nuances a Learner Must Become Aware Of

1. A right to win is relative, never absolute — name the rival or the claim is empty

Most weak right-to-win memos never name a competitor. They say "we are well positioned" or "our data is an advantage," sentences that sound like claims but cannot be tested, because there is nothing to test them against. A claim is only real once it completes the sentence "we win because we have X, and [named rival] does not, because Y." Meera's memo was defensible precisely because it said Vidisha, by name, and said what Vidisha would have to do — build the same six years of integrated hospital data from scratch — to close the gap.

2. Table stakes are not an advantage, even when they took real effort to build

Every serious hospital-software vendor now carries baseline data-security certification and basic clinical-safety documentation. These cost real money and real months to obtain, which tempts teams into listing them as strengths. They are not a right to win; they are the price of being allowed to compete at all. The test is simple: if every credible rival already has it, or will have it before your launch, it cannot be the reason you win.

3. A right to win belongs to an arena, not to the company as a whole

A company's overall strength does not transfer automatically into a new arena governed by a different buyer. Vaibhav's warm relationship with hospital administrators was a genuine asset in the arena it was built for — renewing the core bed-management contract — and irrelevant in NeuroWatch's arena, where the clinical committee, not the administrator, made the call. Teams that skip re-testing capabilities against the new arena's actual decision-maker routinely carry an advantage across a line where it stops applying.

4. It is a hypothesis to test cheaply, not a conclusion to assert expensively

The discipline right-to-win analysis is meant to instil is finding the cheapest possible test of the claim's riskiest assumption before committing full capital to it. For Meera's team, the riskiest assumption was not the machine-learning model's accuracy; it was how hospital procurement would classify the purchase. A three-hospital, ninety-day pilot tested that assumption for roughly ₹35 lakh, a fifteenth of the full build cost — a much better trade than discovering the answer only after the full team had been staffed for nine months.

5. Durability decays — a right to win has a shelf life, not a permanent status

An advantage validated today is not validated forever. Vidisha's own six years of accumulated clinical trust and hospital relationships were themselves a right to win once, built against smaller, less capitalised rivals; that advantage is now the thing newer entrants, including AI-native monitoring companies, are trying to erode. Any right-to-win memo that does not name a review date, and the specific competitor move that would trigger an early review, is implicitly assuming a permanence that competitive markets do not grant.

6. It is commonly confused with first-mover advantage, but being first is not itself a right to win

Arriving first in an arena earns nothing on its own; it matters only if being first compounds into something hard to copy — accumulated data, switching costs, a network effect, a regulatory relationship — before a better-capitalised fast follower arrives. Vidisha was first into deterioration prediction among India's hospital-software vendors, and that mattered a great deal, but only because six years of being first had compounded into 340 live integrations and a validated clinical model, not because "first" was itself the asset.

7. However well applied, it cannot tell you whether the arena is worth winning, or whether your team can execute

Right-to-win analysis answers one question — can we win this arena relative to these rivals — and deliberately brackets two others. It says nothing about whether the arena is large enough to be worth the effort even if won cleanly, a question that belongs to market sizing, and it says nothing about whether the team assigned to it can actually ship what the analysis assumes, a question that belongs to execution risk. Teams that treat a validated right to win as a green light without separately checking arena size and delivery capability routinely win small arenas well, or lose large ones through poor execution of a genuinely sound plan.

How the Picture Changes by Product Type and Company Stage

In consumer products, right to win most often rests on brand and distribution reach compounding through habitual, low-consideration repeat purchase; the advantage shows up as unaided recall and shelf or app presence rather than a single named decision-maker's committee approval, and the relevant comparison is often against category alternatives more broadly rather than against one point competitor with a name and a sales team. NeuroWatch's B2B, high-consideration sale, by contrast, routes through named committees — clinical, procurement — whose criteria Meera's team could interview directly; a consumer product team rarely gets that clean a conversation and must infer key success factors from behavioural and purchase data instead. In marketplace products, right to win typically hinges on liquidity: enough of one side — say, alert data volume or clinician trust across a critical mass of hospitals — to make the other side's participation self-reinforcing, so the relevant capability question becomes less "can we build a better model" and more "can we reach the liquidity threshold before a rival does," a race dynamic largely absent from Vaibhav's single-institution sale.

The distinction between an early-stage company and a large one is at least as consequential as the distinction between product types. An early-stage company's right to win is usually thin on defensible assets and thick on speed and founder-specific insight; it can credibly claim advantage in an arena an incumbent has not yet noticed is worth entering, because the incumbent's organisational attention, not its capability, is the scarce resource. A large, established company's right to win, by contrast, typically rests on assets accumulated over years — Vaibhav's six years of clean vitals data and 210 live integrations are exactly this kind of asset, unavailable to a two-year-old start-up regardless of how talented its team is — but that same size can become a liability when the arena rewards a speed the large company's own processes cannot match. The practical implication for a team like Meera's is that the honest test changes with which side of that line the company sits on: a start-up should be suspicious of a right-to-win claim built entirely on assets it does not yet have, while an incumbent should be equally suspicious of one built entirely on a speed it has not demonstrated recently.

Common Mistakes

Passion mistaken for capability. The symptom is leadership justifying entry into an arena by saying "we care about this more than anyone" or "this is core to our mission," with no accompanying structural asset. The underlying misunderstanding is that conviction is not itself a capability a rival cannot copy; it produces no cost, speed, or trust advantage that a competitor's own motivated team could not also generate. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask whether a resourced rival's product team, on hearing your full plan, would shrug or scramble to respond — conviction without a named structural asset usually earns a shrug.

Capabilities collected without being matched to the arena's actual key success factors. The symptom is a strategy memo listing four or five strengths, none of which appear when customers, unprompted, explain why they actually chose a vendor. The underlying misunderstanding is that teams default to capabilities that are easy to measure internally — headcount, feature count, capital raised — rather than the capabilities customers use to decide. The diagnostic is to run the list against verbatim win/loss interview transcripts; a capability that never appears in a customer's own explanation of a purchase decision probably is not one.

Treating a validated right to win as permanent. The symptom is that no one on the team revisits the original analysis, and the company is caught flat-footed when a rival closes a gap that was real two years earlier but was never re-tested. The underlying misunderstanding treats durability as a yes-or-no attribute established once, rather than a decaying quantity that needs a review date. The diagnostic is to put an explicit shelf-life on every right-to-win memo — reassess by a named date, or immediately if a named rival takes a specific action — and to calendar it like any other commitment.

Testing the claim against "the market" instead of the specific next-most-likely responder. The symptom is a memo that says "no one else offers this," true today, while ignoring an adjacent player with the assets to pivot in quickly. The underlying misunderstanding treats the absence of a current competitor as the same thing as the absence of a capable future one. The diagnostic is to name the three players most able to enter within twelve months, given their existing assets, and to simulate what each would actually need to do to erase the advantage.

What Good Looks Like

What separates a right-to-win memo that survives a hard board question from one that collapses under it is not polish; it is whether the team went looking for the weakest link in its own claim before someone else did. That discipline, increasingly, described what Meera's team did over the following two weeks: naming Vidisha specifically instead of gesturing at "the competitive landscape"; interviewing eleven CMOs rather than assuming clinical trust would transfer; running the unfavourable second-pass arithmetic voluntarily rather than waiting for a board member to demand it; and being willing to say, in front of the same board that wanted a clean yes, that one assumption — how hospitals would actually route the purchase — was unverified and cheap enough to test before ₹2.31 crore was committed. That last move, proposing a bounded test of the riskiest assumption rather than either a full commitment or a full retreat, is usually the clearest outward signal that a team understands right to win as a claim to be earned under uncertainty, not a phrase to invoke for permission to build something it already wanted to build.

The question a right-to-win memo owes its reader is never "is this good," but "compared to whom, and why can't they simply do it too."

What Meera Decided, and Two Questions Worth Sitting With

Meera's board memo recommended neither a full green light nor a rejection, but a staged bet: a ninety-day pilot with three hospitals already on Vaibhav's core platform, chosen specifically to test whether NeuroWatch would in fact route as a low-friction add-on or as a full new-vendor evaluation, before committing the full ₹2.31 crore and nine-person team implied by the first-pass case. The reasoning was direct. The underlying right-to-win claim — Vaibhav's existing integration depth and six years of clean vitals data reducing both integration friction and validation time relative to Vidisha — was real and matched to the arena's actual key success factors; the analysis had passed the match test and the relative-advantage test cleanly. But its economics depended entirely on one specific, testable assumption that had not yet been tested, and testing it with three hospitals over ninety days would cost roughly a fifteenth of the full build. If the pilot confirmed the favourable routing, Meera's team would return to the board with the ₹4.72 crore case validated by real hospitals rather than by eleven CMO interviews. If it did not, Vaibhav would have spent ninety days and about ₹35 lakh finding that out, rather than nine months and ₹2.31 crore.

What the memo did not resolve, deliberately, was whether Vaibhav's advantage would still be worth pursuing once Vidisha, Dozee, or one of the global monitoring companies responded to Vaibhav entering the arena at all — a question that belongs to the next topic worth reading, moats and the 7 Powers, which asks how a right to win, once established, is defended over years rather than months. A second, related question — what happens to a right-to-win claim built on proprietary data and integration depth when a capable rival can assemble something comparable using open models and open data — belongs to competing with open source and free, and is worth reading precisely because it stress-tests the most common way a right-to-win claim quietly expires without anyone noticing the moment it happened.

Question one. For the arena you are evaluating right now, can you name the one or two capabilities that make you more likely to win it than a specific, named rival — in a single sentence, not a slide of five bullet points — and if you cannot, do you actually have a right to win, or only a reason to want one?

Question two. Which of the capabilities on your own list would your closest competitor's product lead, reading your memo over your shoulder, immediately recognise as something they already have too — and how would your conclusion change if that list were cut in half?

Builds on The product strategy document — right to win is the document's claim of advantage.

case20v1-comp.differentiation:
Diwan Home Collective: The Right to Win

A teaching case on competitive strategy and the right to win · Product Management, ISB

1. Opening

On the morning of 6 October 2026, Kabir Saxena sat in his office above the Diwan Home Collective workshop in Jaipur's Sanganer industrial belt, re-reading a WhatsApp message from a board observer sent at 11 the previous night. Diwali, the biggest furniture-buying window of the Indian retail year, was five weeks away, and the festive marketing and inventory budget had to be locked at the board call on 13 October. Kabir had one week to recommend how Diwan should respond to a rival on the Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) selling furniture that looked, in a photograph, almost identical to Diwan's best-selling designs — at 30 to 40 per cent lower prices. The question was not really about price. It was which of Diwan's assets a machine-made competitor could not copy, and whether the next twelve months would be built on that asset or quietly abandon it.

2. Company background

Kabir founded Diwan Home Collective in 2019 after eight years managing export orders for a Jodhpur furniture-making family business. Diwan buys finished pieces on contract from roughly 1,400 artisan family units across four clusters — sheesham and mango-wood joinery in Jodhpur, brass and bone inlay in Saharanpur, block-printed upholstery in Jaipur, and pierced-metal work in Moradabad — grades and photographs every piece in-house, and sells across India through its own app, marketplaces, and since January 2026 through ONDC. Where a factory runs one design down a production line, Diwan runs small batches through many workshops, using its own inspectors, a colour-matching database and a two-week delivery promise to make handcraft feel as reliable as anything mass-produced. Its declared competitors — Pepperfry, Urban Ladder (part of Reliance Retail since 2020), Nilkamal, and IKEA India's online store — source primarily from factories; Diwan has always priced 20 to 35 per cent above them on comparable categories, on the promise that a piece is handmade, traceable to a named artisan cluster, and customisable in wood tone, fabric and dimension. Revenue reached ₹168 crore in the year ended March 2026 (Exhibit 1), up from ₹123 crore, and Diwan closed a 2023 Series B in which Dhanvriddhi Growth Partners, a Bengaluru growth-equity fund, took a board seat.

3. The situation

In June 2026, Dhaatu Furniture Works — a CNC-manufacturing group based in Faridabad that had until then sold to hotels and builders — opened a consumer storefront on ONDC and its own app, offering machine-carved furniture styled to resemble popular handcrafted designs, close enough to specific Diwan bestsellers that Ovais Contractor's team had flagged two listings to legal counsel for a possible design-registration complaint. Dhaatu had just closed a ₹140 crore Series C led by Dhanvriddhi Growth Partners — the same fund that sat on Diwan's board. In the eleven weeks before Dhaatu's storefront went live, Diwan's ONDC orders had been growing nine per cent week-on-week; in the eleven weeks after, growth fell to one per cent, and the ONDC search rank of Diwan's ten highest-volume listings slipped from an average of third to an average of ninth, because ONDC's default sort weights heavily toward price. Meenal Deshmukh, who owns the marketplace and ONDC relationship from Mumbai, said three regional resellers serving hospitality clients had asked, in the same week, whether Diwan could offer anything closer to Dhaatu's price point. Ovais, from Jodhpur, was clear the clusters were already near festive-season capacity; the only way to grow volume quickly was machine-assisted components for a subset of designs — precisely what Dhaatu did.

4. The people

Kabir Saxena — Founder & CEO, Jaipur. Wants to keep Diwan's promise of handmade, traceable furniture; worried price-matching tells customers the craft story was negotiable.
Meenal Deshmukh — VP, Marketplaces & Growth, Mumbai. Owns the ONDC and marketplace revenue line; wants a lower-priced sub-brand fast, before the search-rank damage compounds.
Ovais Contractor — Head of Artisan Network & Supply, Jodhpur. Knows the 1,400 family units cannot scale on demand without quality loss or machine assistance; wants any decision to respect what the network can deliver.
Priyanka Bose — Partner, Dhanvriddhi Growth Partners, Bengaluru; board observer at Diwan and the partner who led Dhaatu's Series C. Wants Diwan to defend its growth rate, and sees matching Dhaatu's entry price as the fastest way — a view her fund's stake in both firms does nothing to discourage.
