6. The options

Option A – Hold the line. Keep the catalogue Signature-only, concede share on ONDC, and redirect a third of the ₹18 crore festive marketing budget — ₹6 crore — into artisan-story and provenance content rather than performance ads. The likely cost: ONDC revenue falls an estimated 36 per cent, from the ₹14 crore run-rate to about ₹9 crore, as price-led buyers move to Dhaatu. The upside: Signature keeps its 50 per cent gross margin and 38 per cent two-year repeat rate (Exhibit 2) untouched, and Diwan spends nothing chasing a customer it was never trying to keep.

Option B – Launch a Diwan Value line. Commission a CNC-assisted line at Moradabad, priced within 15 per cent of Dhaatu, at ₹9 crore of capex. Modelled on Exhibit 2's Value row, a first-year target of 25,600 orders at ₹12,500 brings ₹32 crore of revenue at a 30 per cent margin, or ₹9.6 crore of gross profit. But pilot-city data suggests roughly a third of Value buyers — about 8,500 of the 25,600 — would otherwise have bought Signature. On those, Diwan trades a ₹9,200 margin for a ₹3,750 one, giving up about ₹4.63 crore it already had; only the remaining 17,100 orders, worth about ₹6.41 crore of margin, are genuinely new. Net new gross profit is closer to ₹1.8 crore against ₹9 crore of capex — a weak return, and one that puts Diwan's name on a machine-cut line for the first time.

Option C – Reposition upward and exit the price fight. Withdraw from ONDC and the lowest marketplace tier — together about ₹32 crore, 19 per cent of FY26 revenue — and redirect the freed capacity, roughly a quarter of the 1,400 family units, into a made-to-order premium collection at ₹27,600, 50 per cent above Signature's ₹18,400, sold only through Diwan's app and two curated design marketplaces, with export shipping for NRI buyers in Dubai and Singapore. A 90-day pilot suggests about ₹21 crore of incremental revenue at a 58 per cent margin, or ₹12.18 crore of gross profit. Net revenue dips about ₹11 crore, from ₹168 crore to about ₹157 crore, but what remains is built on the artisan network rather than against it.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, can Diwan do that Dhaatu Furniture Works cannot easily copy — and what can Dhaatu copy that Diwan has been pricing as if it could not?
  2. Read Exhibit 2 closely: what does the gap between Signature's and Dhaatu's gross margins tell you about what each company is actually selling?
  3. Does Dhanvriddhi Growth Partners holding stakes in both Diwan and Dhaatu change what Priyanka Bose's advice is worth, and how should Kabir handle that?
  4. Which option would you recommend to the board on 13 October, and what would you tell Ovais Contractor to prepare the artisan network for?

8. A note for the learner

A right to win is not a claim that a company is better in general; it is a claim that it holds some capability, relationship or asset a specific rival cannot quickly replicate, and that the market rewards. This topic asks you to name that asset precisely enough to tell whether a given move strengthens it or spends it down. Diwan's right to win is not "handcrafted furniture" as a slogan — Dhaatu can put a similar photograph online in a week. It is the 1,400 contracted artisan family units, the grading and colour-matching system built around them, and the two-year repeat-purchase behaviour (38 per cent, against Dhaatu's 14 per cent) that combination earns. Judged only on FY27 revenue growth, Option B looks best, since it is the only one that adds volume quickly. But Exhibit 2's arithmetic shows its real first-year return is thin — about ₹1.8 crore of new margin for ₹9 crore of capex — because a third of its buyers are Diwan's own customers trading down, and every unit sold at Dhaatu's price and cost structure teaches the market that the craft premium was negotiable.

The defensible path is Option C, with one piece of Option A folded in: withdraw from ONDC and the bottom marketplace tier rather than fight Dhaatu there, redirect the freed artisan capacity into the higher-margin made-to-order tier the network was always suited to, and spend the marketing budget on the provenance story that supports that price rather than on defending a channel Diwan cannot win on its own terms. It costs about ₹11 crore of top line in year one — the real price of not confusing growth with advantage — and leaves the one asset a machine cannot replicate, the artisan network and what it has taught customers to expect, larger rather than smaller.
case40v1-comp.differentiation:
Upkaran Factory Cloud: What Exactly Is Ours?

A teaching case on the right to win · Strategy & Business: Competitive Strategy & Moats · Product Management, Indian School of Business

1. Sunday night, Coimbatore

The north-east monsoon arrived early in 2026, and on the night of Sunday 4 October the rain on the roof behind Upkaran Factory Cloud's office on Avinashi Road was loud enough that Sharmila Venkataraman gave up on the call with Toronto and switched to typing. Two documents were open. The first was the next morning's board agenda: one item, “FY28 plan and channel strategy — decision required”. The second was a letter from Udaygiri Textile Machinery, dated 26 June, giving notice that it would not renew the original-equipment agreement expiring on 31 March 2027, offering instead to keep Upkaran inside its machines as an unbranded analytics engine on a sixty-two per cent revenue share. An answer was due by 15 October.

Upkaran had closed FY26 with ₹186 crore of revenue, 955 instrumented plants and the most-cited product in Indian spinning. Sharmila had spent nine years telling investors, customers and her own engineers what its advantage was, and had believed it every time. What she could not now do was say which of the four things she had told them was true — the physics of the breakage models, the install base, the field engineers who could wire a forty-year-old ring frame in three days, or the traceability ledger European accounts had begun asking about. Each reading of the evidence pointed to a different answer on Monday, each argued by someone she trusted.

2. Company history, and the agreement of March 2021

Upkaran was founded in Coimbatore in 2017 by Sharmila, then a process engineer six years into the floors of a Tiruppur spinning group, and Vikram Chhabra, a data scientist met at a Ministry of Textiles workshop. The founding observation was narrow and correct: Indian mills spinning Shankar-6 and other domestic cottons live with far more fibre variability than European mills on uniform imported lots, so the generic monitoring software sold by global equipment makers — tuned on that uniformity — produced alerts Indian supervisors learned to ignore. Between 2017 and 2019 Upkaran hand-instrumented thirty-eight mills across Tamil Nadu, Gujarat and Punjab, its engineers sitting through shifts labelling end-breakage events by cause. The result, 2.7 lakh labelled events, is still called the gold set.

The decision that shapes everything available in 2026 was taken in March 2021. Udaygiri Textile Machinery, a Coimbatore builder of ring frames and auto-coners with about a fifth of the domestic new-machine market, offered to pre-install Upkaran on every frame it shipped and sell it through its dealers. Upkaran's plant count tripled in eighteen months. The price was three clauses. Udaygiri took thirty per cent of subscription revenue and owned the customer relationship. Clause 6.2 barred Upkaran's own edge gateway from any Udaygiri machine for the term plus twenty-four months. Clause 11.4 granted Udaygiri a perpetual licence to “machine telemetry and derived annotations” from channel plants — a phrase drafted, in 2021, to cover warranty diagnostics.

3. The industry

India's spinning sector is large, fragmented and thin-margined: several thousand mills, mostly family-controlled, clustered around Coimbatore, Tiruppur, Ahmedabad and Ludhiana, selling yarn into a domestic knitwear base and into export chains ending with European and American brands. Capital equipment comes from a handful of builders — Lakshmi Machine Works domestically, Swiss and German houses at the top end — all of whom now ship monitoring software with the machine. Policy pushes capacity and formalisation at once, through the production-linked incentive scheme and GST e-invoicing.

Two external forces bear on the product. The European Union's ecodesign regime and its Digital Product Passport will oblige brands importing textiles to carry verifiable information about a garment's production chain, pushing traceability down to spinning — where fibre from many farms becomes one lot. The other is the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023: Upkaran's shift-productivity module attributes machine events to operator identifiers, and in July 2026 one customer's works committee asked what consent basis applied — a question Anoushka Rege's team in Berlin had raised in 2024.

Upkaran faces three kinds of rival, which is part of the problem. Omkaar Plant Intelligence, a Pune company that raised ₹410 crore in January 2025, is horizontal: it sells monitoring to auto components, pharma and food plants, and entered spinning with breadth Upkaran cannot match. Udaygiri is vertical and owns the iron. The global industrial platforms are neither, but they are what a mill's foreign customer's consultants recommend. Upkaran's seventy-four international plants, in Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia and the Gulf, exist largely because Umm Suqeim Textile Trading LLC, a Dubai sourcing house, began asking suppliers for lot-level data in 2024 and named Upkaran as an acceptable way to provide it.

4. The situation in detail

Through 2022 and 2023 Upkaran read its numbers as vindication of the channel. Plants acquired through Udaygiri renewed at ninety-eight per cent, the highest of any channel and still the highest (Exhibit 2), at a fraction of the cost of direct selling. The FY26 plan assumed the channel would carry volume while direct sales carried value, and the Series C of ₹270 crore raised in November 2024 at ₹1,850 crore post-money was priced on a plant-count curve only the channel could produce.

Three things have since turned out to be wrong, and they arrived within seven months of each other.

In February 2026 Udaygiri launched Udaygiri Pulse, its own monitoring product, free for three years with the machine's annual maintenance contract. In August, a usage audit ordered by Jaideep Narang found the ninety-eight per cent renewal figure measured almost nothing: channel renewals were bundled inside Udaygiri's AMC invoice and rolled over undecided, and 165 of the 402 channel plants — forty-one per cent — had never opened the quality module. Weekly active supervisors averaged six per channel plant against thirty-four in direct accounts. On 22 September, Vikram Chhabra re-ran the model comparison the sales deck had used for two years, this time letting Pulse retrain on Udaygiri's fleet telemetry rather than be tested cold. On domestic cotton the gap narrowed from 0.71 against 0.44 to 0.68 against 0.61. Vikram's note ran four lines. The last read: “Our edge may have been the labels, not the method, and clause 11.4 may already have given them the labels.”

Two law firms have since opined on clause 11.4. A Chennai firm holds that “derived annotations” covers only warranty diagnostic flags, not Upkaran's cause-coded breakage labels, which are original work. A Mumbai firm engaged by Odhani Growth Capital reads it as covering anything derived from channel telemetry, labels included, and warns that litigation would take three years and end any renewed relationship. Neither has seen Udaygiri's training data, and neither can say whether the question is moot.

5. The people

Sharmila Venkataraman, co-founder and CEO, Coimbatore. Believes the advantage is domain depth in spinning. Incentive: a 2028 exit above the Series C preference. Not saying: she suspects what she has called a technology moat is an operations moat — the field force — which makes Upkaran far less valuable than the board thinks.
Rukmini Iyengar, CFO, Bengaluru. Wants the white-label signed: ₹96 crore of cash against ₹4.2 crore of monthly burn leaves under twenty-three months, and the FY28 plan of ₹310 crore is unreachable without the channel. Incentive: clean books for a Series D. Not saying: her own model shows channel contribution falling at once, and she has not circulated it.
Jaideep Narang, SVP Engineering, Pune. Wants to go horizontal — weaving, garmenting, auto components — arguing that a platform with one vertical is a feature, not a company. Incentive: sixty more engineers. Not saying: two of his four strongest leads have offers from Zoho and Omkaar, and a big build keeps them.
Vikram Chhabra, co-founder and Chief Data Scientist, Toronto. The most pessimistic voice on the model edge, and insistent the gold set be re-measured first. Incentive: intellectual honesty, and four years in Toronto off the mill floor. Not saying: he thinks the real asset is the channel plants' data, which makes leaving worse than anyone has modelled.
Anoushka Rege, Head of Product Design, Berlin. Argues the traceability ledger is the only differentiation a customer's customer will pay for, and that European brands, not mills, are the buyer. Incentive: a product with a global surface. Not saying: her evidence is twelve conversations with sourcing managers, none holding a budget.
Deepa Krishnamoorthy, Director, Customer Success (International), Singapore. Ran the twenty-two loss interviews and trusts them over the CRM. Incentive: renewals where there is no field presence. Not saying: three of her largest Bangladesh accounts run on Udaygiri machines, and a public fight puts them at risk.
Manohar Palanisamy, Head of Plant Deployment, Tiruppur. Runs 212 field engineers across fourteen states at about ₹20.4 crore a year. Believes the field force is the moat and resents its billing as a cost line. Incentive: headcount, and a team rivals cannot hire quickly. Not saying: FY26 attrition in his group ran high enough that the number has left the monthly pack.
Tanvi Malhotra, Partner, Odhani Growth Capital, Bengaluru; board member since the Series C. Wants growth held above thirty per cent and is impatient with what she calls “moat theology”. Incentive: a mark-up inside her fund's window. Not saying: the fund is raising its next vehicle, and a written-down Upkaran is expensive for her personally.

8. The options as Sharmila sees them

Sign the white-label. Upkaran becomes the engine inside Udaygiri Pulse at thirty-eight per cent of subscription revenue instead of seventy: on ₹54 crore of channel ARR, ₹20.5 crore retained rather than ₹37.8 crore, a ₹17.3 crore cut from day one. Against it, Udaygiri commits to 420 new plants over three years, about ₹21.4 crore of retained ARR at the channel's ₹13.4 lakh a plant. The brand disappears from 402 mills, and with it the line to the supervisor whose behaviour the product exists to change.

Go horizontal. Jaideep's plan: ₹110 crore over eighteen months to extend the platform to weaving, garmenting and auto-component plants, sixty more engineers, a breadth contest with Omkaar. It answers Tanvi's growth requirement and Manohar's retention problem at once, spends every rupee Rukmini is counting, and asks a company whose only evidence of advantage is one process to compete where it has none.

Go deeper and narrower. Abandon the channel, keep the direct and international business, and reprice around outcomes: a share of the realisation and waste savings the product produces. The six-plant pilot at Ullas Spinning Group measured about ₹1.9 crore of annual saving per plant; a thirty per cent share is ₹57 lakh a plant, just above Exhibit 2's ₹54.8 lakh average direct ARR, against the ten per cent, or ₹19 lakh, the mills' procurement heads counter with. Four of the six pilot plants changed cotton mix mid-measurement.

Sell the passport. Build the traceability ledger as the product at ₹6 lakh a plant a year: across all 955 plants, ₹57.3 crore; at the ₹1.8 lakh median premium mills say they would pay, ₹17.2 crore. The build costs ₹46 crore over two years, and the buyer who wants it — the European brand, or Umm Suqeim's sourcing desk — is not a party Upkaran has ever invoiced.

Sharmila had drawn the four as a two-by-two, and noticed on Friday that the grid held no square for what Ilango Sivasubramanian described, nor for Vikram's worry that the channel plants are the training corpus rather than a revenue line — which makes the first option a data decision in commercial clothes. 9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Udaygiri requires an answer by 15 October 2026; the agreement lapses on 31 March 2027, and clause 9.1 obliges nine months' notice of any transition of channel accounts — already running out. Clause 6.2 bars Upkaran's gateway from Udaygiri machines until March 2029, so walking away does not mean taking the 402 plants along. Cash is ₹96 crore against ₹4.2 crore of monthly net burn, just under twenty-three months, and the board's FY28 plan of ₹310 crore sits against a trajectory of about ₹236 crore in FY27 and ₹290 crore in FY28 if the channel stays flat. Ullas Spinning Group, 38 plants and ₹22 crore of ARR — 10.8 per cent of the total — holds a most-favoured-pricing clause, so any list-price cut defending the channel propagates into the largest direct account. The DPDP consent question is unresolved, with a design review on 14 October.
